summary: Children complete the missing half of a symmetric figure across a given mirror line (a butterfly, a pattern on squared paper, or a shape) point by point, and verify by folding along the line so the halves coincide. The core idea: every point of the drawn half has a partner the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror; joining these partners in the same order reconstructs the whole as a true mirror image (sense reversed, not a slid copy). The fold test is both the construction method's justification and its self-check. Progress from vertical to horizontal and later sloping mirror lines, holding the 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule constant.
misconceptions: Completing the figure by eye so the reflected points are not equidistant from the mirror line.
Sliding a copy of the half across (translating) rather than reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image.
Miscounting the squares, so individual partner points land the wrong distance from the mirror.
Duplicating or shifting points that lie on the mirror line instead of leaving them fixed.

activities.title: Build the butterfly's missing wing, point by point
steps: Start from half a butterfly drawn on squared paper beside a clearly marked vertical mirror line.
For each key point of the given half (e.g. a wingtip), count the squares perpendicular from the mirror line to that point.
Count the SAME number of squares straight out on the far side, perpendicular to the mirror, and mark the partner point.
Repeat for every corner/key point, then join the partners in the SAME order as the original half.

Fold the paper along the mirror line (holding it up to the light if needed), or stand a mirror/Mira on the line and compare the reflection of the given half with your drawn half. Check that the two halves line up, allowing for small inaccuracies in drawing and folding.
If the fold misses anywhere, find the slipped point, re-count its squares on both sides, and correct it.
activities.insight: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side; building partner-by-partner (counting equal perpendicular distances) and folding to check turns a 'looks about right' sketch into a construction you can justify and check.

activities.title: Reflect, don't slide: spot the difference
steps: Look at two completions of the same half-butterfly: one where the second wing points the opposite way, one where a copy of the left wing has been slid across so both wings point the same way.
Decide which is truly symmetric and explain how you can tell.
Fold each along the mirror line and watch which one's halves coincide.
Say what folding reveals about the slid copy (the wingtips miss).
activities.insight: Reflection reverses 'sense' — a true mirror image faces the opposite way, unlike a shape merely slid (translated) across, which keeps the same orientation and, for a lopsided half like a butterfly wing, will not fold onto the original half.

activities.title: Points on the line, and new mirror directions
steps: Work a figure that has a key point sitting right ON the mirror line; decide where its partner goes (it stays put — distance zero, not duplicated or shifted).
Complete a figure whose mirror line is HORIZONTAL, counting squares perpendicular to that line (now up/down).

Later, try a figure with a SLOPING mirror line (on squared paper, a diagonal line at 45°), keeping the same rule: each partner the same perpendicular distance from the line, counted in corner-to-corner diagonal steps across the squares.
Fold (or imagine the fold) along each mirror line to check the halves coincide.
activities.insight: The 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule is constant whatever the mirror's orientation; points on the line are fixed, and the method generalises from vertical to horizontal and sloping lines.

activities.title: Check and choose: deciding if a completion is correct
steps: On a grid, complete a given half by marking the partner points and joining them.
From several completed figures, pick the correctly reflected one, rejecting a wrong version that is the half slid across (same orientation) and another where a point is one square off.
Decide whether folding a figure along the mirror line would make the halves match, and say yes or no.
Justify each choice by counting squares or by predicting the fold.
activities.insight: Being able to recognise correct reflections — and name exactly why the slid-copy and one-square-off versions are wrong — consolidates the perpendicular-equidistant and sense-reversal rules.

checkQuestion: Give the child squared paper showing half a simple symmetric figure (say the left half of a butterfly or a simple flag pattern) with a clearly marked vertical mirror line, plus one figure whose mirror line is horizontal. Say: 'Complete each figure so the whole thing is symmetrical about the mirror line. When you have finished, check your work.' Set the task and WATCH how the second half is built and whether the child checks by folding — do not explain the method.
checkAnswer: The child builds the missing half point by point — each partner point the same number of squares perpendicular from the mirror line as its original, joined in the same order — so the completed figure is a true mirror image (sense reversed), leaves any on-the-line points fixed, and works for the horizontal mirror as well as the vertical. The child verifies by folding along the mirror line (or imagining the fold) so the halves coincide.
